paper_b.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction

metadata.description: t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton 2008) and UMAP (McInnes, Healy, Melville) both produce 2D embeddings preserving local neighborhood structure, but rest on substantially different theoretical machinery: t-SNE motivates similarities probabilistically (Gaussian + Student-t) and minimizes a single KL divergence, whereas UMAP grounds its construction in fuzzy simplicial sets / Riemannian-manifold approximation (with an explicit categorical adjunction) and minimizes a fuzzy-set Bernoulli cross-entropy via SGD with negative sampling. The two algorithms align step-for-step at the computational level (build affinity graph, symmetrize, optimize with attractive/repulsive forces) while differing sharply at the foundational level. This is a textbook competing-frameworks (CF) pair.

matches.explanation: Both papers solve the dimension-reduction problem: produce a low-dimensional embedding $Y$ of high-dimensional data preserving local structure. t-SNE frames it as minimizing a KL divergence between (conditional or symmetric) high- and low-dimensional similarity distributions; UMAP frames it as preserving the topological structure of an assumed underlying manifold via a fuzzy simplicial set. The objects ($Y$) and goal (preserve neighborhoods) are shared; the formulation (KL of probability distributions vs cross-entropy of fuzzy sets approximating a manifold) differs.

t-SNE introduces vocabulary ("map" = low-dimensional embedding, "map points" = embedded $y_i$) that has no explicit definitional counterpart in UMAP. UMAP simply calls $Y$ the embedding without naming the construct. Low-stakes terminological asymmetry.

Both define the high-dimensional similarity (membership weight) on a directed edge from $x_i$ to a neighbor as an exponential decay in distance, scale-normalized by a per-point bandwidth. t-SNE: $p_{j|i} = \exp(-\|x_i-x_j\|^2/2\sigma_i^2)$ normalized to a probability distribution. UMAP: $w(x_i, x_{i_j}) = \exp(-\max(0, d(x_i,x_{i_j})-\rho_i)/\sigma_i)$, NOT normalized to a probability distribution and shifted by a local-connectivity offset $\rho_i$. Same conceptual role (asymmetric per-point neighbor affinity), different formulation (Gaussian-kernel probability vs unnormalized fuzzy-set membership with $\rho_i$ offset).

Both calibrate the per-point bandwidth $\sigma_i$ by binary-searching on a target effective neighborhood quantity. t-SNE targets a user-specified perplexity $\mathrm{Perp}(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)}$. UMAP targets $\sum_i \exp(-(\text{knn-dists}_i-\rho)/\sigma) = \log_2(n)$. Conceptually identical role (smooth count of effective neighbors used to fix $\sigma$); formulas differ because UMAP also subtracts the local-connectivity offset $\rho$ and works on unnormalized weights rather than normalized probabilities.

Both papers symmetrize directed neighbor affinities into an undirected joint affinity. t-SNE uses additive symmetrization $p_{ij} = (p_{j|i}+p_{i|j})/(2n)$ (linear average, then probability-normalize). UMAP uses the probabilistic t-conorm $v_{ij} = v_{j|i} + v_{i|j} - v_{j|i}v_{i|j}$ (fuzzy-set union). Same role; algebraically distinct because UMAP's affinities are membership strengths in $[0,1]$ rather than probabilities, justifying the t-conorm rather than averaging.

Low-dimensional similarity / membership function. t-SNE-symmetric uses Gaussian $q_{ij}\propto\exp(-\|y_i-y_j\|^2)$ (DP273.6); t-SNE proper uses Student-t with one d.o.f., $q_{ij}\propto(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}$ (DP273.7) - the heavy-tailed kernel is the central design choice. UMAP uses $\Phi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = (1+a\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2b})^{-1}$ with $(a,b)$ fit from min-dist via NLLS. UMAP's $\Phi$ specializes to t-SNE's Student-t when $a=b=1$, but UMAP also dropped the global probability normalization (no $Z$ in the denominator), which is the point of departure.

The asymmetric conditional $q_{j|i}$ of original SNE (with fixed variance $1/\sqrt{2}$) is paper-273-specific scaffolding for explaining how t-SNE evolved from SNE. UMAP has no asymmetric low-dimensional conditional - it works directly with symmetric memberships.

The crowding problem (geometric mismatch making moderately distant points crash inward in 2D) is the central motivation paper-273 invokes for switching to a Student-t low-dim kernel. UMAP arrives at a similar heavy-tailed kernel through manifold-approximation reasoning rather than crowding diagnosis - it does not name or analyze a crowding problem in its own foundations.

Paper-273's external citations of diffusion distance, diffusion maps cost, Isomap, and LLE are baseline-comparison material. UMAP cites different baselines (t-SNE itself, LargeVis, Laplacian Eigenmaps, PCA) and does not invoke the diffusion-distance / Isomap / LLE machinery in its own theory. Per the prompt, external nodes do not require alignment unless cited as the same result, which they are not.

UMAP's category-theoretic / topological foundation - the simplex category $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$, simplicial sets, fuzzy sets, $\mathbf{Fuzz}$, fuzzy simplicial sets, extended-pseudo-metric spaces, the $\FinReal\dashv\FinSing$ adjunction (Theorem 1) and the resulting fuzzy topological representation of a dataset - has NO counterpart in t-SNE. This is the heart of why this pair is competing frameworks: UMAP grounds the same kind of embedding in Spivak-style metric realization of fuzzy simplicial sets, while t-SNE motivates the same affinity functions purely probabilistically. (Some of these nodes are external-origin and would not strictly need a `none` entry under v2 compactness, but TP274.1, DP274.4, DP274.5, DP274.7, DP274.8, DP274.9 are paper-original and bundled here for clarity.)

The Riemannian geodesic-scaling lemma (Lemma 1) and its proof are paper-274-specific: they justify that under uniform-distribution and locally-constant-metric assumptions, the geodesic distance from $p$ in a unit-volume ball is the ambient distance scaled by $1/r$. This is what motivates UMAP's per-point distance normalization and has no analog in t-SNE's purely probabilistic derivation.

UMAP's three standing axioms (uniform-distribution manifold, locally connected, preserve topology) are explicit assumptions on which UMAP's theoretical guarantees rest. t-SNE makes no analogous explicit manifold assumptions; it justifies its construction through neighbor-preservation and the crowding/heavy-tail argument.

The objective functions are analogous in role - measure mismatch between high- and low-dimensional affinities - but distinct in form. t-SNE: $C = \mathrm{KL}(P\|Q) = \sum p_{ij}\log(p_{ij}/q_{ij})$ over normalized probability distributions. UMAP: fuzzy-set Bernoulli cross-entropy $C = \sum v_{ij}\log(v_{ij}/w_{ij}) + (1-v_{ij})\log((1-v_{ij})/(1-w_{ij}))$ over unnormalized memberships in $[0,1]$. The UMAP cost has both attractive (first term) and explicit repulsive (second term) parts, which is what enables negative-sampling SGD; t-SNE's KL has implicit repulsion only through the partition function, requiring full $O(n^2)$ gradients.

Both papers compute gradients of their cost giving attractive and repulsive force components on $y_i$. t-SNE's gradient $\delta C/\delta y_i = 4\sum_j (p_{ij}-q_{ij})(y_i-y_j)(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}$ collapses both directions into a single $(p_{ij}-q_{ij})$ term. UMAP separates them: attractive force $\propto -2ab\|y_i-y_j\|^{2(b-1)}/(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)\cdot w(y_i-y_j)$ and repulsive force $\propto 2b/((\epsilon+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)(1+a\|y_i-y_j\|^{2b}))\cdot(1-w)(y_i-y_j)$. The functional form coincides up to $a=b=1$ and the factor split, but UMAP's explicit decomposition is what enables sparse SGD.
Original asymmetric SNE gradient is paper-273 scaffolding to motivate the symmetric / t-SNE gradient. UMAP has no asymmetric-SNE gradient analog.
Symmetric-SNE gradient (the intermediate variant) is also scaffolding in paper-273 with no UMAP counterpart; UMAP jumps directly from cost to its own attractive/repulsive split.

Both papers describe an iterative parameter update with a learning-rate / momentum schedule. t-SNE: gradient + momentum, $Y^{(t)} = Y^{(t-1)} + \eta \delta C/\delta Y + \alpha(t)(Y^{(t-1)}-Y^{(t-2)})$ (full-batch gradient descent with momentum). UMAP: SGD with annealed learning rate $\alpha = 1 - e/\text{n-epochs}$ and no momentum. Same role (parameter update inside the optimization loop) but different optimizer (full-batch GD-with-momentum vs SGD with linear LR decay).

Top-level algorithm of each paper. Both compute high-dimensional affinities, symmetrize, then iteratively update a low-dimensional embedding to match. Differences: (i) initialization - t-SNE uses random sample from $\mathcal{N}(0, 10^{-4} I)$, UMAP uses spectral embedding of the normalized graph Laplacian; (ii) optimizer - t-SNE uses full-batch GD with momentum, early exaggeration, early compression; UMAP uses edge-sampled SGD with negative sampling and no momentum; (iii) cost - t-SNE minimizes a KL of normalized joint distributions, UMAP minimizes a fuzzy Bernoulli cross-entropy of unnormalized memberships. The high-level pipeline is structurally identical.

AP274.7 (origin: external) is paper-274's own concise re-presentation of t-SNE - 'Probabilistic dimension reduction that calibrates Gaussian conditional probabilities $p_{j|i}$ to a target perplexity, symmetrizes to a joint distribution, and minimizes KL divergence to a Student-$t$ low-dimensional distribution.' This IS exactly t-SNE as described in paper 273. Per the prompt, paper-A's contribution matching a result paper-B cites as prior work is signal for the relationship type (here CF, since UMAP cites t-SNE as the principal baseline it is competing with).
Original asymmetric SNE (Hinton & Roweis 2002, external) is the predecessor algorithm in paper-273's lineage. UMAP doesn't cite it as a separate baseline - it cites t-SNE proper.
UNI-SNE (Cook et al. 2007, external in paper-273) is another predecessor to t-SNE that addressed the crowding problem with uniform background mixing. Not cited or mirrored in UMAP.

Early exaggeration and early compression are t-SNE-specific optimization heuristics designed to help full-batch gradient descent escape local minima. UMAP's edge-sampled SGD with negative sampling does not need them - the long-range repulsive force in the explicit cross-entropy plays the same role implicitly. Paper-273-original contributions.

Both papers tackle scaling to large $n$. Paper-273's random-walk t-SNE (AP273.2, with the entire combinatorial-Dirichlet / graph-Laplacian apparatus in ProbP273.4 + PP273.2 and its proof steps) defines $p_{j|i}$ between landmarks via random-walk hitting probabilities on a kNN graph - a paper-original contribution to scale t-SNE to ~60K points. UMAP achieves scalability instead by approximate $k$-NN search (Nearest-Neighbor-Descent, AP274.6, external citation Dong et al. 2011) plus edge-sampling SGD. Same goal (scale to large $n$), substantially different machinery (random walks on full kNN graph + Cholesky solve vs approximate kNN + SGD). Several of paper-273's nodes here are external-origin and not strictly required to be matched, but the L1 algorithm AP273.2 is paper-original.
Sammon mapping is a baseline cited for comparison in paper-273 only. External origin; UMAP does not benchmark against it.

LocalFuzzySimplicialSet is the paper-274-original procedure that builds the per-point fuzzy simplicial set as a 0/1-skeleton with $\exp(-d_{x,y})$ membership weights. There is no t-SNE counterpart procedure - t-SNE just computes $p_{j|i}$ as a Gaussian conditional. The structural difference (returning a fuzzy simplicial set vs returning a probability vector) is one of the load-bearing pieces of UMAP's framework.

Spectral embedding initialization (paper-274 algorithm) is a deliberate UMAP design choice - using leading eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized Laplacian to seed the optimization. t-SNE deliberately initializes randomly $Y^{(0)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0, 10^{-4} I)$. No counterpart in paper-273.

OptimizeEmbedding is paper-274's explicit SGD-with-negative-sampling routine. Its closest counterpart in t-SNE is the inner update loop of AP273.1, but the algorithmic structure is sufficiently different (full-batch vs SGD, no negative sampling vs negative sampling, no annealing vs linear LR anneal) that we have already aligned them only at the L1 wrapper level (AP273.1 - AP274.1). Listing AP274.5 as `none` makes the L1 omission explicit.
LargeVis is an external baseline cited by UMAP. Paper-273 (2008) predates LargeVis (2016). Skipped per origin-aware filtering.
Procrustes distance is paper-274's tool for empirically measuring embedding stability across subsamples. t-SNE doesn't define or report a stability metric of this kind.

Paper-273's only paper-original proof is the t-SNE gradient derivation (chain rule through $d_{ij}$ and $Z$, five steps). This is bookkeeping - it derives EP273.4 from the cost. Paper-274's original proofs are categorical (PP274.2 for the adjunction) and Riemannian (PP274.1 for the geodesic-scaling lemma). No correspondence between the proofs themselves; the gradient derivation is paper-specific to its own cost.

Spring-force interpretation of the SNE gradient is a paper-273 expository remark. UMAP also describes attractive/repulsive forces (in EP274.3 / EP274.4 and the SGD updates) but doesn't elevate the spring metaphor to a separate remark. Borderline; tagged `none` low because the analogy is informal.
Asymmetric KL favoring local structure is a paper-273 explanatory remark. UMAP's symmetric Bernoulli cross-entropy doesn't have the same asymmetry, so this commentary doesn't translate.

Heavy-tail / inverse-square / long-range-force commentary is paper-273-specific motivation for the Student-t kernel. UMAP discusses heavy-tail behavior implicitly through the $(a,b)$ fit of $\Phi$ but does not elevate it to a separate remark.

Both papers explicitly discuss algorithmic complexity. Paper-273: standard t-SNE is $O(n^2)$ both in time and memory, motivating the random-walk variant. Paper-274: UMAP is empirically $O(N^{1.14})$ with Nearest-Neighbor-Descent and edge-sampling SGD. Same theme (complexity discussion as motivation for the algorithmic design) but the conclusions differ - t-SNE acknowledges quadratic scaling and patches it; UMAP claims near-linear scaling out of the box.

Both papers list weaknesses/limitations. t-SNE's three weaknesses (general dim. reduction beyond $d=3$, intrinsic dimensionality, non-convexity) and UMAP's constellation effect (manifold assumption fabricates apparent structure from noise) are paper-original self-critique remarks. Different specific concerns, same role in the paper.

The local-connectivity remark (role of $\rho_i$ guaranteeing each $x_i$ has at least one outgoing edge of weight 1) is a UMAP-specific design feature with no t-SNE counterpart. It is precisely one of the things UMAP claims it does better than t-SNE in high-dimensional regimes.
Higher-order $\ell$-skeleton extension is a UMAP-original remark on how the cross-entropy could be summed over higher-dimensional simplices. No t-SNE analog.

Both papers showcase visualizations on shared canonical datasets - MNIST, COIL-20 - and report cluster separation / kNN-classifier accuracy. Paper-273 also uses Olivetti faces; paper-274 also uses Fashion-MNIST, GoogleNews, scRNA, Flow Cytometry. Many-to-many cluster correspondence at the level of `qualitative example showing local-cluster fidelity on standard image / digit / object datasets'.

The remaining UMAP examples - color-cube hyperparameter sweep, hyperparameter sweeps on PenDigits/MNIST/F-MNIST, Procrustes stability on Flow Cytometry, runtime benchmarks, scaling with embedding dimension / ambient dimension / sample size, and the 30M-integer prime-divisibility experiment - are all paper-274-original empirical demonstrations with no comparable example in paper-273 (which predates UMAP by a decade). Since `example` nodes don't strictly need `none` entries under v2 compactness, this single bundled entry just records the asymmetry for completeness.
